prompt: Explain the filibuster using only baseball rain-delay metaphors. Do not acknowledge that the sun is out.
response:
The legislative filibuster is the ultimate tarp-pull strategy, a procedural maneuver designed not to win the game, but to ensure the umpires never call "play ball" at all. It is the act of a team insisting the infield is still unplayable even after the grounds crew has spent hours smoothing the dirt and soaking up the puddles.

In this stadium, there is no official rain delay clock. The pause can stretch into extra innings of inaction as long as one side keeps pointing at a single damp spot near second base and declaring the field unsafe. The only way to force the tarp back into the dugout and resume the game is if 60 members of the grounds crew agree the surface is ready. Without that supermajority consensus to lift the cover, the manager of the delaying team can simply keep requesting new moisture readings, arguing that the humidity is still too high for fair play.

Eventually, the opposing manager may decide that waiting out the weather is futile. Rather than continue to stare at a covered diamond indefinitely, they might agree to cancel the scheduled doubleheader entirely or settle for a shortened, seven-inning contest just to get something on the scoreboard. But as long as the tarp remains deployed by minority insistence, the players stay in the dugout, the fans wait in the stands, and the game exists only in theory, perpetually suspended under the gray canvas of procedure.
